note: Display names and poles for the scores. Scores run from -100 (minus pole) to +100 (plus pole). 'balanced' axes weight left-coded and right-coded questions equally; see scripts/revisions/rev_2026_10_14_sim_fixes.py.

overall.name: Overall
overall.about: Your overall position, from every question that splits along today's left–right line.
bands: You take the left side on nearly every issue that divides the parties today.
You take the left side on most issues that divide the parties, with some exceptions.
You split your answers across the left–right line, or sit near the middle on many issues.
You take the right side on most issues that divide the parties, with some exceptions.
You take the right side on nearly every issue that divides the parties today.

axes.name: Taxes and redistribution
axes.about: How much government should use taxes and transfers to narrow the gap between rich and poor.
bands: Much higher taxes on the wealthy and large transfers, to sharply narrow the gap between rich and poor.
Somewhat more redistribution: higher taxes at the top and a stronger safety net.
Roughly today's mix of taxes and transfers, with targeted changes either way.
Somewhat lower taxes and leaner transfers, favoring growth and work over redistribution.
Low taxes and minimal transfers; incomes should be set by markets and private effort, not government.

axes.name: Business and labor rules
axes.about: How much government should set rules for businesses, workers and markets.
bands: Strong rules for business: powerful unions, high minimum wages, tough antitrust and consumer protection.
More worker and consumer protection than today, with business still largely private.
A mix: keep most current rules, trim some, add a few.
Fewer rules on business and hiring; regulations often cost more than they save.
Free markets with very light regulation; let contracts, competition and courts handle most problems.

axes.name: Health care and retirement
axes.about: Whether health care and retirement should run mainly through public programs or private choices.
bands: Health care and retirement as public guarantees: single-payer care, expanded Social Security.
Bigger public role: a public option, expanded Medicaid and protected benefits.
Keep the current public–private mix and fix it at the edges.
More private choice: market-based plans, accounts and limits on program growth.
Mainly private provision; government's role should be a narrow safety net at most.

axes.name: Housing and growth
axes.about: Whether to let more homes be built (overriding local limits) or protect existing neighborhoods.
bands: Override local limits so far more homes get built, including apartments in single-family areas.
Loosen zoning and permitting to allow more housing, with some local say.
Mixed: more building in some places, local control in others.
Let communities keep their character; growth should be gradual and locally decided.
Protect existing neighborhoods from densification; local control over land use comes first.

axes.name: Trade
axes.about: Open trade with low tariffs versus protecting American industry and jobs.
bands: Open trade: low tariffs and trade deals, because they lower prices and grow the economy.
Mostly free trade, with some protections and help for workers who lose out.
Case by case: open trade with allies, protection for key industries.
Use tariffs to protect American jobs and industry, even if prices rise somewhat.
Broad tariffs and economic nationalism; bring production home whatever the cost.

axes.name: Environment and energy
axes.about: How hard to push on climate and the environment, and how much cost to accept for it.
bands: Act fast and at scale on climate, accepting real costs and limits on fossil fuels.
Steady climate action through investment and regulation, minding the cost.
Act on climate where it's cheap; keep energy affordable and reliable.
Keep energy cheap and the economy growing; climate rules should be modest.
Prioritize cost and growth; most climate regulation does more harm than good.

axes.name: Technology and AI
axes.about: How tightly to regulate AI, social media and other technology.
bands: Regulate AI and big tech tightly: licensing, liability, and breaking up the largest firms.
Clear rules for AI and social media, especially for safety, kids and competition.
Some targeted rules, but mostly wait and see.
Light-touch rules so innovation isn't slowed; fix specific harms as they appear.
Let technology develop freely; regulation mostly protects incumbents and slows progress.

axes.name: Privacy
axes.about: How much monitoring and data collection to allow for security and law enforcement.
bands: Strong privacy rights: warrants for nearly everything, strict limits on data collection and surveillance.
Lean toward privacy, with surveillance allowed under clear court oversight.
Balance privacy and security case by case.
Allow more monitoring and data use for security and law enforcement.
Broad surveillance powers are worth it to stop crime and terrorism.

axes.name: Abortion and moral issues
axes.about: Abortion and other moral questions: personal choice or traditional moral rules in law.
bands: Personal choice on abortion and other moral questions; the law shouldn't enforce moral rules.
Mostly personal choice, with some limits (for example later in pregnancy).
Mixed: some limits and some choice, depending on the issue.
Law should protect traditional moral standards on most of these issues, with some exceptions.
Traditional morality in law: abortion banned or nearly so, moral rules enforced.

axes.name: Sexuality and gender identity
axes.about: Same-sex marriage, transgender policy and how the law should define sex and gender.
bands: Full legal recognition of gender identity, and same-sex marriage as settled.
Support same-sex marriage and most transgender protections, with some exceptions (for example sports).
Mixed: accept same-sex marriage but cautious on some gender identity policies.
Law should mostly follow birth sex; skeptical of gender identity policies in schools and sports.
Traditional definitions of sex, marriage and family in law.

axes.name: Religion in public life
axes.about: How much room religion should have in schools, government and public life.
bands: Strict separation of church and state: no religion in public schools or government.
Mostly separate, with room for private religious expression and accommodation.
Accommodate religion in public life without favoring it.
More room for religion in public life: school prayer options, broad religious exemptions.
The nation's laws and public life should reflect its religious heritage.

axes.name: Family and gender roles
axes.about: Views on marriage, child-rearing and men's and women's roles.
bands: Fully egalitarian roles; policy should support every family form equally.
Mostly egalitarian, open to different family arrangements.
Mixed views on marriage, child-rearing and men's and women's roles.
Traditional family arrangements usually work best and deserve support.
Marriage and traditional roles are central and should be favored by policy and culture.

axes.name: Race and equity
axes.about: How to address racial gaps: group-conscious remedies or colorblind rules.
bands: Active group-conscious remedies for racial gaps: affirmative action, targeted programs, reparations.
Some group-conscious policies alongside universal ones.
Mixed: universal programs, with some targeted help.
Mostly colorblind rules; help should go by need, not race.
Strictly colorblind law and policy; race-conscious programs should end.

axes.name: Immigration
axes.about: How many immigrants to admit and how to treat people here without legal status.
bands: Much more immigration and a broad path to citizenship; deportations rare.
More legal immigration and a path to citizenship, with border enforcement.
Roughly current levels, with both enforcement and legalization for some.
Less immigration, tougher enforcement, legal status only in limited cases.
Sharply cut immigration and deport people here illegally.

axes.name: National identity
axes.about: What it means to be American: shared ideals and pluralism, or a common culture.
bands: America is defined by its ideals and its diversity; no single culture is the national one.
Shared ideals matter most, and diversity is a strength.
Both shared ideals and a common culture matter.
A common culture and language hold the country together.
National identity rests on a shared culture, language and heritage that should be preserved.

axes.name: Crime and policing
axes.about: Policing, prisons and punishment versus reform and rehabilitation.
bands: Major reform: shrink policing and prisons, focus on rehabilitation and root causes.
Reform-minded: fewer people in prison, more accountability for police.
Both reform and enforcement, depending on the problem.
Support police and firm punishment, with some reforms.
More policing and tougher sentences; public order comes first.

axes.name: Guns
axes.about: Gun rules, from strict control to broad gun rights.
bands: Strict gun control: licensing, registration, bans on many weapons.
More gun rules such as universal background checks and some weapon limits.
Some added rules, but protect ordinary gun ownership.
Protect gun rights; most new rules burden law-abiding owners.
Broad gun rights with few restrictions; the right to bear arms is near absolute.

axes.name: Drugs and vice laws
axes.about: Whether drugs, gambling, sex work and assisted dying should be legal for adults or prohibited.
bands: Adults should be free to use drugs, gamble, sell sex or end their lives as they choose.
Mostly legal and regulated, with limits on the riskiest choices.
Mixed: legal for some choices, prohibited for others.
Mostly prohibited, with room for medical use and narrow exceptions.
Drugs, gambling, sex work and assisted dying should stay illegal and be enforced.

axes.name: Health and safety rules
axes.about: Whether government should require or discourage things for health and safety: vaccines, helmets, vapes, sugary drinks.
bands: Adults and parents decide about vaccines, helmets, raw milk and other health risks; no mandates.
Mostly individual choice, with a few rules like school vaccines.
Mixed: some health and safety mandates make sense, others go too far.
Health and safety rules are usually worth it, from school vaccines to vape limits.
Strong public-health rules: mandates, bans and taxes that steer people away from health risks.

axes.name: Free speech
axes.about: How far to protect offensive, false or hateful speech, counted evenly across speech the left dislikes and speech the right dislikes.
bands: Protect almost all speech, including offensive, false and hateful speech.
Strong free speech, with narrow limits.
Protect most speech but limit some clearly harmful kinds.
Harmful, false or hateful speech should face real limits.
Broad limits on harmful speech are needed to protect people and society.

axes.name: Presidential power
axes.about: How much power presidents should have, and how much to rely on courts and checks.
bands: Strong checks and balances: limit presidential power, respect courts and institutional rules, whoever is president.
Lean toward checks on the president, with room to act in emergencies.
Balance presidential action with checks.
Presidents should have more room to act without Congress or courts.
A strong executive that can act decisively, even past traditional limits.

axes.name: Elections
axes.about: Voting rules and election reform: expanding access versus tightening security and keeping traditions.
bands: Make voting as easy as possible and reform elections (mail voting, automatic registration, new systems).
Expand access, with reasonable security.
Balance access and security.
Tighten security (voter ID, cleaner rolls), keep traditional election methods.
Strict security and traditional voting in person on Election Day.

axes.name: Trust in government
axes.about: How much you trust government to be honest and competent, whoever is in charge.
bands: Government is mostly honest and competent, whoever is in charge.
Fairly trusting of government, with some doubts.
Mixed trust in government.
Fairly distrustful of government's honesty and competence.
Deep distrust of government, whoever is in charge.

axes.name: Trust in experts and media
axes.about: How much you trust scientists, experts, news organizations and official statistics.
bands: Trust scientists, experts, the news media and official statistics.
Mostly trust experts and the media, with some skepticism.
Trust some experts and sources, not others.
Skeptical of experts, mainstream media and official numbers.
Deep distrust of experts, mainstream media and official institutions.

axes.name: Populism
axes.about: Whether the system mostly works or is rigged by the powerful.
bands: The system mostly works; elites and institutions mostly act in good faith.
The system works, though it often favors the powerful.
Mixed: some of the system works, some is rigged.
The system is tilted toward elites and insiders.
The system is rigged by elites; ordinary people need to take it back.

axes.name: Federalism
axes.about: Whether big decisions should be made nationally or left to states and cities, counted evenly across cases where state power helps the left and where it helps the right.
bands: National standards on most big issues; states shouldn't set their own rules on rights.
Lean toward national rules, with state flexibility on details.
Some issues national, others left to states.
Lean toward states and cities deciding most things.
State and local control over nearly everything the Constitution doesn't reserve to Washington.

axes.name: Education
axes.about: Who should run schools and what they teach: public systems and educators, or parents and school choice.
bands: Strong public schools run by educators; no vouchers; curriculum set by professionals.
Mostly public system and professional control, with some parental input.
A mix of public schools, choice and parental say.
More school choice and parental control over what's taught.
Full school choice with public money following the child; parents decide what's taught.

axes.name: Global engagement
axes.about: Working through allies, aid and international bodies versus going it alone.
bands: Work through allies, international bodies, treaties and aid.
Mostly work with allies and institutions, keeping some independence.
Engage with the world selectively.
Put America first; be wary of treaties, aid and international bodies.
Go it alone: leave or ignore international bodies, cut foreign aid.

axes.name: Use of force
axes.about: How readily to use military force abroad and how big a military to keep.
bands: Military restraint: smaller military, force only as a last resort.
Cautious about force, with a strong enough defense.
Use force when clearly needed, keep a strong military.
Ready to use force to protect interests and allies; a big military.
Use force readily and keep overwhelming military power.

axes.name: China
axes.about: How hard to compete with and confront China: trade, ownership, technology and Taiwan.
bands: Treat China like any other country: trade freely and cooperate on shared problems.
Engage China, with limits on sensitive technology.
Compete with China and protect key industries, but keep talking and trading.
Treat China as a serious rival: limit trade, ownership and technology sales.
China is the main adversary: cut ties, block investment and confront it on every front.

axes.name: Underlying values
axes.about: The values under your views: equality and change versus order, tradition and authority.
bands: Equality and change come first; tradition and authority often stand in the way.
Lean toward equality and change, with some respect for tradition.
A balance of equality, change, order and tradition.
Lean toward order, tradition and authority, with openness to change.
Order, tradition and authority come first.

FED.note_L: states and cities pursuing left-leaning policies
